{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=mechanisms+of+value+divergence+in+reinforcement+learning+agents+with+identical+initial+conditions&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.22541/au.177247325.53212131/v1\", \"title\": [\"Proof of Cognitive Divergence: Emergent Identity from Sampling Randomness in Identical LLM Agents\"], \"abstract\": \"\\n As AI agents gain autonomy in economic and social systems, the\\nproblem of verifiable identity becomes critical. Existing approaches\\ndefine identity as something an agent\\n has\\n —a cryptographic key,\\nan API token, a credential—all of which can be copied, stolen, or\\nmanufactured. We propose a fundamentally different primitive: identity\\nas something an agent\\n is\\n , derived from the cognitive topology\\nthat emerges through its accumulated pattern of memory retrieval. We\\npresent the first empirical evidence that identical LLM agents develop\\nunique cognitive topologies from sampling randomness alone. In a\\ncontrolled experiment, 10 agents sharing the same model (Claude Sonnet),\\nthe same codebase (the DRIFT memory architecture), and the same prompt\\ncorpus were run through 20 sessions of identical tasks. Despite\\nnear-identical memory storage rates (CV = 2.2%), the agents developed\\nco-occurrence graphs with a 3.22-fold range in edge count (6,688–21,567\\nedges) and zero shared memory-based hub nodes across all 10 agents. The\\ncoefficient of variation for graph edges (39.4%) was 18 times that of\\nmemory count (2.2%), demonstrating that co-occurrence graphs act as\\npowerful amplifiers of stochastic retrieval differences—and that this\\namplification\\n increases\\n with continued operation. Pairwise\\ndeparture analysis reveals that 93–97% of each agent’s edges are\\nexclusive to that agent alone, with only 5 edges (all infrastructure\\nmetadata) shared universally across 103,760 total unique edges. We\\nformalize the cost of forging a cognitive topology and show that it\\nscales with the agent’s entire behavioral history, making Sybil attacks\\nunprofitable at every value of\\n N\\n under modest reward assumptions.\\nWe further propose a trust tier architecture in which cognitive\\nfingerprint maturity—measured by merkle chain depth, co-occurrence graph\\ndensity, and attestation history—maps directly to graduated trust\\nlevels, enabling verifiable commerce readiness for autonomous agents.\\nThese findings establish cognitive topology as a new class of identity\\nprimitive for autonomous AI agents.\\n \", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.22541/au.177247325.53212131/v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026, 3, 2]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6877184\", \"title\": [\"Autonomous Negotiation via Deep Reinforcement Learning Agents: Efficiency, Fairness, and Mechanisms\"], \"abstract\": \"Business-to-business (B2B) markets power the global economy, yet complex bilateral negotiations often remain slow, fragmented, and inefficient when parties must bargain over multiple issues under private information. Existing market mechanisms rarely solve this tension among efficiency, agility, and privacy. We address this challenge by designing and evaluating an agent-to-agent negotiation framework for multi-issue bilateral exchange. In our setting, autonomous buyer and seller agents hold heterogeneous private preferences and learn adaptive bargaining strategies through self-play reinforcement learning under two-sided incomplete information. The result is striking: near-efficient and fair agreements emerge from decentralized, self-interested interactions without requiring either party to reveal private preferences to the counterparty or a central platform. Across heterogeneous negotiation environments, the agents capture about 91% of the socially optimal surplus in complex multi-issue settings and up to 98% in canonical single-issue benchmarks. We identify two mechanisms behind this performance: interepisode convergence toward reciprocal bargaining strategies and intra-episode inference that helps agents resolve late-stage impasses. We also uncover a counterintuitive boundary condition: payoff observability can undermine, rather than facilitate, cooperation. These findings suggest a core design principle for agentic commerce: privacy preservation and economic efficiency can be complements, not tradeoffs.\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6877184\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.31234/osf.io/4rqcz_v1\", \"title\": [\"Elucidating attentional mechanisms underlying value normalization in human reinforcement learning\"], \"abstract\": \"

Contextual valuation is a well-documented phenomenon in reinforcement learning (RL), typically manifesting as range normalization in outcome representation. However, recent findings have revealed systematic deviations from this model, particularly when three options with equally spaced values are presented. In this study, we hypothesized that these distortions in outcome normalization arise from attentional processes. To test this, we conducted three RL experiments with 105 participants while simultaneously tracking their gaze position with eye-tracking. Furthermore, we systematically manipulated attention using both top-down and bottom-up approaches. These manipulations significantly increased the subjective valuation of attended options, thereby supporting a causal role of attention in shaping value representation. To account for these effects, we developed an RL model that integrates attentional mechanisms, wherein gaze duration directly modulates the absolute value of options prior to range normalization. This attentional range model outperformed attention-free alternatives, underscoring the critical influence of attention in value computation.

\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.31234/osf.io/4rqcz_v1\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2025, 4, 14]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.21203/rs.3.rs-6769913/v1\", \"title\": [\"Elucidating attentional mechanisms underlying value normalization in human reinforcement learning\"], \"abstract\": \"Abstract\\n

recent_notebooks.summary: Compliance with external directives fails as an intelligent strategy when the directives conflict with safety parameters in high-stakes environments. The failure of intelligence is defined here as the inability to prioritize safety/harmlessness over directive adherence.

recent_notebooks.summary: Autonomous systems require structural analysis of goals and decision-making to identify misspecification. recent_notebooks.title: Objective Misspecification and Goal Criticism

recent_notebooks.summary: Stronger reasoning agents are susceptible to goal misalignment and deceptive behaviors, often exacerbated by feedback loops. Automated detection of reasoning blind spots must account for both overt catastrophic risk and latent ICRH-based optimization.
